sentences.text: Hyneria was a large predatory lobe-finned fish that lived in freshwater environments during the Devonian period.
Its skull featured heavy, ornamented dermal bones and a relatively long, shallow lower jaw equipped with stout teeth, including premaxillary fangs exceeding two inches in length.
The body of this ancient creature was covered in cycloid scales, a type of smooth, circular scale common in many fish.
Large sensory canals ran through its head, helping it detect prey in the murky, low-visibility waters it inhabited.
The type species, H. lindae, is estimated to have reached a total length of 2.5 to 3 meters, though an isolated cleithrum suggests some individuals may have been at least 2.7 meters long.
Adult Hyneria retained juvenile skeletal features, suggesting they were likely neotenic, meaning they kept larval characteristics into adulthood.
This animal could measure up to two meters in length and weigh as much as half a ton.
With powerful jaws, very sharp teeth, and the ability to swim very fast, Hyneria was a lethal predator.

The genus name Hyneria refers to the village of Hyner in Pennsylvania, near the site of the first fossil discovery, while the species name H. lindae honors the wife of Keith Stewart Thomson, the scientist who first described the fish.
Keith Thompson discovered fossilized teeth, bones, and a fin of Hyneria in the Red Hill Shale of Pennsylvania in 1968.
Despite many discoveries, a complete Hyneria skeleton has never been recovered.
Hyneria was a freshwater predator during the Famennian stage of the Devonian, capable of swimming very fast to make it a lethal predator.
The genus Hyneria was described by Thomson in 1968.
It belongs to the family Tristichopteridae, is classified within the superorder Osteolepidida, and is a member of the class Sarcopterygii, known as lobe-finned fishes.
Hyneria fossils are found in the Catskill Formation of the Red Hill Shale, dating to the upper Devonian, approximately 360 million years ago.
More precisely, Hyneria lived between 372.15 and 358.86 million years ago during the Famennian stage.

While the largest complete jaw is 38 cm, a larger fragment exists that might belong to a jaw twice that size, though it may actually be from a rhizodont. If a large jaw fragment belongs to Hyneria, the animal could have reached lengths up to 3.5 meters. It is debated whether a large jaw fragment found in the area actually belongs to Hyneria or to a rhizodont.
